title: Range Sum Query - Immutable
description:
# Range Sum Query - Immutable

Given an integer array `nums`, handle repeated range-sum queries on the same array.

Implement the `NumArray` class:

* `NumArray(int[] nums)` initializes the object with the array `nums`.
* `int sumRange(int left, int right)` returns the sum of the elements from index `left` through index `right`, inclusive.

The array is immutable after construction: there is no operation that changes an element of `nums`. Every query is guaranteed to satisfy `0 <= left <= right < nums.length`.

In operation examples, the first array lists operations and the second lists their argument lists, paired by index and executed left to right. The first operation constructs the object; later operations use that same object. Outputs align by index too: constructors and void methods produce `null`; an empty argument list `[]` means no arguments.

## Example 1:

**Input:**
["NumArray", "sumRange", "sumRange", "sumRange"]
[[[-2, 0, 3, -5, 2, -1]], [0, 2], [2, 5], [0, 5]]

**Output:**
[null, 1, -1, -3]

**Explanation:**
`sumRange(0, 2)` returns `(-2) + 0 + 3 = 1`.
`sumRange(2, 5)` returns `3 + (-5) + 2 + (-1) = -1`.
`sumRange(0, 5)` returns `(-2) + 0 + 3 + (-5) + 2 + (-1) = -3`.

## Constraints:

* `1 <= nums.length <= 10^4`
* `-10^5 <= nums[i] <= 10^5`
* `0 <= left <= right < nums.length`
* At most `10^4` calls will be made to `sumRange`.

solutions.name: Prefix Sum Array
solutions.description:
## Approach

Build a one-based prefix sum array where `prefix[i + 1]` stores the sum of `nums[0]` through `nums[i]`. A query `[left, right]` is answered by subtracting the prefix before the interval from the prefix after the interval.

## Key Insight

Because the array never changes, every query asks for the difference between two fixed cumulative sums. The extra leading zero avoids special cases for ranges that start at index `0`.

## Complexity Analysis

Initialization takes O(n) time. Each `sumRange` call takes O(1) time. The prefix array uses O(n) extra space.

solutions.name: Fenwick Tree Without Updates
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n log n) init, O(log n) query
solutions.description:
## Approach

Insert each array value into a Binary Indexed Tree during construction. To answer `[left, right]`, compute the tree prefix sum up to `right + 1` and subtract the tree prefix sum up to `left`.

## Key Insight

A Fenwick tree is normally used for mutable prefix sums, but it is also a valid static teaching route. It exposes the same prefix-difference idea while showing how range sums can be decomposed into low-bit buckets.

## Complexity Analysis

Building with point additions takes O(n log n) time. Each query reads two Fenwick prefixes in O(log n) time. The tree uses O(n) space.

solutions.name: Static Segment Tree
solutions.description:
## Approach

Build a segment tree whose nodes store sums of fixed subarrays. `sumRange` recursively skips nodes outside the query, returns nodes completely inside it, and splits only when a node partially overlaps the query.

## Key Insight

Even without updates, the segment tree is a useful contrast to prefix sums: it answers range sums by combining disjoint stored intervals instead of subtracting two cumulative totals.

## Complexity Analysis

The tree is built in O(n) time. Each query visits O(log n) relevant tree levels in this static range-sum setting. The tree array uses O(n) space.

solutions.name: Block Decomposition
solutions.description:
## Approach

Copy the array, split it into blocks of about `sqrt(n)` elements, and precompute each block sum. A query directly scans the partial block at each end and adds full block sums in the middle.

## Key Insight

Block decomposition sits between direct scanning and full prefix sums. It keeps the original values visible while reducing repeated work for long ranges.

## Complexity Analysis

Initialization takes O(n) time. A query touches at most two partial blocks plus the complete blocks between them, so it takes O(sqrt(n)) time. Stored values and block sums use O(n) space.

solutions.name: Direct Scan Baseline
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store a copy of the input array. For each query, loop from `left` to `right` and add the elements one by one.

## Key Insight

This is the simplest correct baseline and is useful pedagogically because it makes the repeated-work problem obvious. Every faster method improves on this by remembering some aggregate information from construction.

## Complexity Analysis

Construction only copies the array, so it is O(n) time in this implementation. Each query can scan the whole array in the worst case, so it is O(n). The copied array uses O(n) space.
